17.39: At once a change passed through all of them, as though this had actually happened. Each of them was aware that together they made a party in a hollow, on an island, with a shared cause against the fluid world out there. Mrs. Ramsay had been restless while she waited for Paul and Minta to come in, unable, as she felt it, to settle to anything. Now that unease turned into expectation. They must come now. Lily Briscoe, meanwhile, tried to work out where this sudden lift of spirits came from, and she compared it with that moment on the tennis lawn when solid things all at once dissolved and such vast distances opened between people. Here the same effect came from the crowd of candles in the barely furnished room, from the windows with no curtains, and from the bright, masklike look that candlelight gives to faces. A weight had been lifted from them; anything could happen, she felt. They must come now, thought Mrs. Ramsay, her eyes on the door, and in that instant Minta Doyle and Paul Rayley came in, together with a maid holding a great dish in both hands. They were terribly late, Minta said; horribly late. And the two of them made their way to opposite ends of the table.
17.40: “I lost my brooch—my grandmother’s brooch,” Minta said, and there was a note of mourning in her voice; her large brown eyes were swimming, and she looked down, then up, as she took her seat beside Mr. Ramsay. All this stirred his chivalry, and he began to tease her,
17.41: How could anyone be such a goose, he asked her, as to go climbing over rocks with jewelry on?
17.42: In a way she was terrified of him—he was so dreadfully clever. On that first night, when she had been placed beside him and he talked about George Eliot, she had been truly frightened, because she had left the third volume of _Middlemarch_ behind on the train and never learned how it ended. Later, though, the two of them got along perfectly, and she pretended to be even more ignorant than she was, since he enjoyed telling her she was a fool. So tonight, as soon as he laughed at her, her fear was gone. Besides, she had known the moment she walked into the room that the miracle had happened: she was wearing her golden haze. Some days she had it; some days she didn’t. Why it came and why it went she never knew, and she could not even tell whether she had it until she entered a room; then she knew at once, from the way some man looked at her. Yes, tonight she had it, enormously; she could tell from the way Mr. Ramsay ordered her not to be a fool. She sat next to him and smiled.
17.43: So it must have happened, Mrs. Ramsay thought; they are engaged. For a moment she felt something she had never expected to feel again: jealousy. Because her husband felt it as well—the glow coming off Minta. He was fond of these girls, these girls with golden-red hair who had something flying loose about them, something a bit wild and harum-scarum; girls who didn’t “scrape their hair off,” who were not, in his phrase for poor Lily Briscoe, “skimpy.” They had some quality she lacked herself, a luster, a richness, and it drew him, amused him, and made him pick out girls like Minta as his favorites. They were allowed to cut his hair, or braid watch-chains for him, or break in on his work, shouting to him (she could hear them), “Come along, Mr. Ramsay; it’s our turn to beat them now,” and out he would come to play tennis.
17.44: Yet she was not really jealous. It was only that now and then, when she forced herself to look in the mirror, she resented a little having grown old—through her own fault, perhaps. (The greenhouse bill, and all the rest of it.) She was grateful to these girls for laughing at him (“How many pipes have you smoked today, Mr. Ramsay?” and so on), because then he seemed a young man again, a man women found very attractive. He was no longer loaded down, no longer crushed by the greatness of his work and the sorrows of the world and his fame or his failure; he was once more the man she had first known, gaunt but gallant, handing her out of a boat, she remembered, with charming ways like that (she glanced at him, and teasing Minta he looked astonishingly young). As for herself—“Put it down there,” she said, and helped the Swiss girl lower the huge brown pot with the Bœuf en Daube gently onto the table in front of her—as for herself, she liked her dunces. Paul must sit by her; she had saved a place for him. Honestly, she sometimes thought the dunces were the ones she liked best. They didn’t weary you with their dissertations. These very clever men, how much they missed, after all! How dried-up they became, there was no denying it. As Paul sat down, she thought there was something very charming about him. She loved his manners, and his sharp, clean-cut nose, and his bright blue eyes. He was so thoughtful. Now that everyone was talking again, would he tell her what had happened?
17.45: “We went back to look for Minta’s brooch,” he said, as he sat down beside her. “We”—she needed no more. From the effort, from the way his voice climbed to get over a hard word, she knew it was the first time he had said “we.” “We” did this, “we” did that. They will be saying it for the rest of their lives, she thought. Marthe lifted off the lid with a little flourish, and a wonderful smell of olives and oil and juices rose from the big brown dish. The cook had worked three days on it. And she must be very careful, Mrs. Ramsay thought as she dug into the soft mass, to pick out an especially tender piece for William Bankes. She looked down into the dish, at its glossy sides and its muddle of savory brown and yellow meats, its bay leaves and its wine, and she thought, This will celebrate the occasion. A strange feeling rose in her, whimsical and tender at once, of keeping a festival, as though two emotions had been summoned in her. One was deep—for what could be more serious than the love of a man for a woman, what more powerful or more impressive, when it carries inside it the seeds of death? And at the same time these lovers, these people walking with shining eyes into illusion, had to be danced around mockingly and decked with garlands.
17.46: “It’s a triumph,” Mr. Bankes said, and he put his knife down for a moment. He had been eating with great attention. It was rich; it was tender; it was cooked to perfection. How did she manage such things so far out in the country? he asked. What a wonderful woman she was. All his love and all his reverence had come back to him; and she knew it.
17.47: “My grandmother’s recipe—it’s French,” said Mrs. Ramsay, and her voice rang with pleasure. French, naturally. What they call cooking in England is an abomination, the two of them agreed. It means dropping cabbages into water. It means roasting meat till it turns to leather. It means peeling away the lovely skins of vegetables. “And the skin,” Mr. Bankes put in, “is where all the virtue of the vegetable lies.” And then the waste, said Mrs. Ramsay. What an English cook throws out would feed an entire French family. She felt that William’s affection had returned to her, that all was well again, that the suspense was over and she was free now to triumph and to mock; and, spurred on by this, she laughed and waved her hands about, until Lily thought, How childlike she is, how absurd, sitting up there with all her beauty unfolded in her once more, talking about vegetable skins. There was something frightening in her. Nobody could resist her. In the end, Lily thought, she always had her way. Now she had managed this—Paul and Minta, it seemed, were engaged. Mr. Bankes was having dinner here. She cast a spell over all of them just by wanting things, so simply and so directly. Lily measured that abundance against her own poverty of spirit. Part of it, she supposed, was Mrs. Ramsay’s belief (her face was all lit up—she did not look young, but she looked radiant) in this strange and terrifying thing that had set Paul Rayley, at the center of it, trembling all over, and yet left him remote, absorbed and silent. As she talked about vegetable skins, Mrs. Ramsay, Lily felt, was exalting that thing, worshipping it, holding her hands over it both to warm them and to shelter it; and yet, having brought it all about, she was somehow laughing, leading her victims, Lily felt, to the altar. Now it came over Lily as well—the emotion, the vibration of love. Next to Paul, how unnoticeable she felt! He was glowing, burning; she was aloof and satirical. He was setting out on an adventure; she was moored to the shore. He was launched and heedless; she was alone, left out. And, ready to plead for a share in his disaster, if disaster it was, she asked shyly:
17.49: His smile was the most exquisite smile, clouded with memory, tinted with dreams. He shook his head. “On the beach,” he said.
17.50: “I’m going to find it,” he said. “I’ll get up early.” Because Minta was not to know, he dropped his voice, and his eyes went to where she sat laughing next to Mr. Ramsay.
17.51: Lily wanted to declare, violently, outrageously, how much she longed to help him. She imagined herself on the beach at dawn, the one who swooped on the brooch lying half-hidden by a stone, and so found herself counted among the sailors and adventurers. But what was his answer to her offer? With a feeling she rarely allowed to show, she actually said, “Let me come with you”; and he laughed. He might have meant yes, or no—perhaps either. It was not his meaning that mattered, though; it was that odd chuckle, as if he had said, Go and throw yourself off the cliff if you want, it’s nothing to me. He turned the heat of love on her cheek—its horror, its cruelty, its lack of all scruple. She was scorched by it. Then, looking down the table at Minta being charming to Mr. Ramsay, Lily flinched on Minta’s behalf, exposed as she was to those fangs, and felt thankful. At any rate, she told herself, her eye falling on the saltcellar in the pattern, she did not have to marry, thank Heaven; that humiliation was not for her. She had been spared that watering-down. She would move the tree a little more toward the middle.
17.52: That was how complicated things were. Because what happened to her, particularly when she stayed with the Ramsays, was that she was made to feel two contrary things, violently, both at once. One said, that’s what you feel; the other said, that’s what I feel; and then the two fought it out in her mind, as they were doing now. Love is so lovely, so thrilling, that I tremble on its brink and, quite unlike myself, volunteer to hunt for a brooch on a beach; and love is also the stupidest, most savage of human passions, and it takes a nice young man with a profile like a cameo (Paul’s profile was exquisite) and turns him into a bully with a crowbar (he was swaggering, he was insolent) in the Mile End Road, in the East End of London. And yet, she told herself, odes have been sung to love since the dawn of time, wreaths and roses have been piled up for it, and nine people out of ten, if you asked them, would say this was the one thing they wanted; while all along the women, to judge by her own experience, would be feeling, This isn’t what we want; nothing is more boring, more childish, more inhuman than love; and yet it is beautiful as well, and necessary. Well then? Well then? she asked, somehow expecting the others to take up the argument, as though in an argument of this kind you fired off your own small bolt, which obviously fell short, and left the rest to the others. So she listened once more to their talk, in case they shed some light on the question of love.
17.53: “And then,” said Mr. Bankes, “there’s that liquid the English call coffee.”
17.54: “Oh, coffee!” said Mrs. Ramsay. But the real question, much more, was one of real butter and clean milk (she was thoroughly roused, Lily could see, and was speaking very forcefully). With warmth and eloquence she laid out the wickedness of the English dairy system and the condition milk was in when it reached your door, and she was just about to prove her charges, having gone into the matter, when laughter broke out all around the table. It started with Andrew in the middle and leaped like fire from one tuft of gorse to the next: her children laughed; her husband laughed; she was laughed at, surrounded by fire, and forced to lower her crest and take down her guns. All she could do in return was point out the table’s mockery and teasing to Mr. Bankes, as an example of what you had to put up with if you attacked the prejudices of the British Public.
17.55: She made a deliberate exception of Lily, though, and did not count her with the rest, because it weighed on her that Lily, who had helped her with Mr. Tansley, was out of things. “Lily agrees with me, anyway,” she said, and in this way drew her in, a little flustered, a little startled. (Lily had been thinking about love.) Both of them were out of things, Mrs. Ramsay had been thinking, Lily and Charles Tansley alike. The glow of the other two made both of them suffer. He plainly felt himself completely out in the cold; with Paul Rayley in the room, no woman would look at him. Poor man! Still, he had his dissertation, on the influence of somebody on something: he could take care of himself. Lily was another matter. Under Minta’s glow she faded, and became even less noticeable than usual, in her little gray dress, with her little puckered face and her little Chinese eyes. Everything about her was so small. And yet, Mrs. Ramsay thought, setting her beside Minta as she appealed to her for support (Lily should bear her out that she went on about her dairies no more than her husband went on about his boots—he could talk about his boots for hours), of the two girls, Lily at forty will be the finer. Lily had a thread of something in her, a flare of something, something all her own, which Mrs. Ramsay liked very much indeed, but which no man would like, she was afraid. Clearly not, unless he were a much older man, like William Bankes. But then he cared—well, since his wife died, Mrs. Ramsay sometimes thought, he perhaps cared for her. Not that he was “in love,” of course; it was one of those unclassified affections, of which there are so many. Oh, but that’s nonsense, she thought; William must marry Lily. They have so much in common. Lily loves flowers. Both of them are cold and aloof and rather self-sufficient. She must arrange a long walk for the two of them.
17.56: It had been foolish to seat them across from each other. That could be fixed tomorrow. If the weather was fine, there should be a picnic. Anything seemed possible. Everything seemed right. Just now (though this can’t last, she thought, standing apart from the moment while the rest of them talked about boots), just now she had arrived at safety. She hovered like a hawk held still in the air; she floated like a flag in an element of joy that filled every nerve of her body, fully and sweetly—not loudly, but rather solemnly, because it came, she thought, as she watched them all eating, from her husband and children and friends. All this, rising in the deep stillness (she was giving William Bankes one very small piece more, and peering into the depths of the earthenware pot), now seemed, for no particular reason, to linger there like smoke, like a vapor drifting upward, keeping them safe together. Nothing needed saying; nothing could be said. There it was, all around them. It had something of eternity in it, she felt, as she carefully served Mr. Bankes an especially tender piece—just as she had felt once already that afternoon about something else. There is a coherence in things, a steadiness; something, she meant, that change cannot touch, and that shines out (she glanced at the window, rippling with reflected lights) against the flowing, the fleeting, the ghostly, like a ruby. So tonight, once more, she had the feeling she had had earlier today, of peace, of rest. It is from moments like these, she thought, that the thing is made that remains forever after. This would remain.
17.57: “Yes,” she told William Bankes reassuringly, “there’s plenty for everyone.”
17.58: “Andrew,” she said, “hold your plate lower, or I’ll spill it.” (The Bœuf en Daube was a complete triumph.) Here, she felt, laying down the spoon, was the still space around the heart of things, where you could move about or rest. She could wait now (everyone had been served), and listen; and then, like a hawk that suddenly drops from its height, she could flaunt and sink easily into laughter, leaning her whole weight on what her husband, at the far end of the table, was saying about the square root of one thousand two hundred and fifty-three, which happened to be the number on his train ticket.
17.59: What did any of it mean? Even now she had no idea. A square root—what was that? Her sons knew. She leaned on them, on cubes and square roots, which was the subject now; on Voltaire and Madame de Staël; on Napoleon’s character; on how land was held in France; on Lord Rosebery; on Creevey’s Memoirs. She let this admirable structure of the masculine mind hold her up and carry her. It ran up and down and crisscrossed like iron girders across the swaying fabric, supporting the world, so that she could give herself up to it entirely, could even close her eyes, or let them flicker for a moment, the way a child lying on its pillow blinks up at the countless layers of leaves on a tree. Then she came to. The building was still going on. William Bankes was praising the Waverley novels.
17.60: Every six months he read one of them, he said. And why should that make Charles Tansley angry? In he rushed (all because Prue won’t be nice to him, Mrs. Ramsay thought) and attacked the Waverley novels without knowing a thing about them, not a single thing, Mrs. Ramsay thought, watching him rather than attending to his words. His manner told her how it was: he wanted to assert himself, and he would always be like this until he had his professorship or had married his wife, and then he would not need to keep on saying, “I—I—I.” Because that was all his criticism of poor Sir Walter Scott—or maybe it was Jane Austen—came to. “I—I—I.” She could hear from his voice, from his emphasis and his uneasiness, that he was thinking of himself and of the impression he made. Success would do him good. Anyway, they were off again, and she did not have to listen now. It would not last, she knew, but for the moment her eyes were so clear that they seemed to travel around the table, effortlessly uncovering each of these people, their thoughts and feelings, like a light slipping under water, so that the ripples and the reeds and the minnows balancing there and the sudden silent trout are all lit up, hanging, trembling. That was how she saw them and heard them. But whatever they said had this quality too, as though their words were like a trout moving while you can see, at the same time, the ripple and the gravel, something on the right, something on the left, and all of it held together. For in active life she would be netting things, sorting one from another; she would be saying that she liked the Waverley novels, or that she hadn’t read them; she would be pushing herself forward. Now she said nothing. For the moment she hung there, suspended.
17.61: “Ah, but how long do you think it will last?” somebody said. It was as if trembling antennae reached out from her, catching certain sentences and pressing them on her notice. This was one. She scented danger to her husband. A question like that was almost sure to lead to some remark that would remind him of his own failure. How long will I be read?—that would be his immediate thought. William Bankes, who was quite free of any such vanity, laughed and said that changes in fashion meant nothing to him. Who could say what would last, in literature or in anything else, for that matter?
17.62: “Let’s enjoy what we enjoy,” he said. To Mrs. Ramsay his integrity seemed altogether admirable. Not for a moment did he seem to think, But what does this mean for me? But if your temperament was the other kind, the kind that needs praise and needs encouragement, then of course you started (and she knew Mr. Ramsay was starting) to grow uneasy, to want someone to say, Oh, but your work will last, Mr. Ramsay, or something of the sort. He made his uneasiness plain enough now, remarking with some irritation that Scott (or was it Shakespeare?) would see him through his lifetime, anyway. He said it irritably. Everyone, she thought, felt slightly uncomfortable, without knowing why. Then Minta Doyle, who had good instincts, declared bluntly and absurdly that she didn’t believe anybody truly enjoyed reading Shakespeare. Very few people, Mr. Ramsay said grimly (though his mind had turned away again), liked it as much as they claimed. Still, he added, some of the plays have considerable merit, and Mrs. Ramsay saw that for now, at least, all would be well. He would laugh at Minta; and Minta, Mrs. Ramsay saw, sensing how intensely anxious he was about himself, would make sure in her own way that he was looked after, and would praise him somehow. But she wished it weren’t necessary; perhaps it was her own fault that it was. In any case, she was free now to listen to Paul Rayley, who was trying to say something about the books you read as a boy. Those lasted, he said. At school he had read some Tolstoy. There was one he never forgot, though he couldn’t remember what it was called. Russian names were impossible, said Mrs. Ramsay. “Vronsky,” said Paul. He remembered that one because he had always thought it made such a good name for a villain. “Vronsky,” Mrs. Ramsay said. “Oh, _Anna Karenina_.” But that did not get them much further; books were not really their line. No—Charles Tansley could correct them both about books in a moment, but with him it was all so tangled up with Am I saying the right thing? Am I making a good impression? that in the end you found out more about him than about Tolstoy. What Paul said, on the other hand, was simply about the thing itself, not about him. Like all stupid people he had a sort of modesty as well, a thought for what you were feeling, and every so often, at least, she found that attractive. At this moment he was thinking neither about himself nor about Tolstoy, but whether she was cold, whether there was a draft on her, whether she would like a pear.
17.63: No, she said, she didn’t want a pear. The truth was she had been jealously guarding the dish of fruit (without knowing it), hoping no one would touch it. Her eyes had been wandering in and out of the curves and shadows of the fruit, among the deep purples of the lowland grapes, then over the horny ridge of the shell, laying a yellow beside a purple, a curved shape beside a round one, not knowing why she did it, or why each time she felt calmer and calmer; until—oh, what a shame that they should do it—a hand stretched out, took a pear, and ruined everything. She looked at Rose in sympathy. She looked at Rose, sitting between Jasper and Prue. How strange that your own child should do such a thing!
17.64: How strange it was to see them sitting there in a row, her children, Jasper, Rose, Prue and Andrew, hardly speaking, but sharing some joke of their own, she guessed, from the way their lips twitched. It was something quite separate from everything else, something they were storing up to laugh at later in their own room. She hoped it was not about their father. No, she thought not. What could it be? she wondered, a little sadly, because it seemed to her that they would laugh when she wasn’t there. All of that was kept hidden behind those rather fixed, still, masklike faces, for they did not easily join in; they were like watchers, like surveyors, raised a little above the grown-ups or set a little apart from them. But looking at Prue tonight, she saw that this was no longer entirely true of her. Prue was just starting, just stirring, just coming down. There was the faintest light on her face, as though the glow of Minta across from her, some excitement, some expectation of happiness, were mirrored in her—as though the sun of the love between men and women were coming up over the edge of the tablecloth, and she, not knowing what it was, leaned toward it and greeted it. Again and again she looked at Minta, shy but curious, so that Mrs. Ramsay looked from one girl to the other and said to Prue inside her own mind, One of these days you will be as happy as she is. You will be far happier, she added—because you are my daughter, she meant; her own daughters had to be happier than other people’s. But dinner was finished. It was time to leave. They were only fiddling with things on their plates. She would wait till they had stopped laughing at some story her husband was telling. He was joking with Minta about a bet. Then she would get up.
17.65: All of a sudden she thought that she liked Charles Tansley; she liked the way he laughed. She liked him for being so angry with Paul and Minta. She liked his clumsiness. There was a good deal in that young man, after all. And Lily, she thought, laying her napkin beside her plate—Lily always has a private joke of her own. You never need to worry about Lily. She waited. She tucked her napkin under the rim of her plate. Well, had they finished now? No. One story had led to another. Her husband was in high spirits tonight; wanting, she supposed, to make up to old Augustus after that business over the soup, he had pulled him in, and the two of them were telling stories about someone they had both known at college. She looked at the window, where the candle flames burned brighter now that the panes had gone black, and as she gazed out there the voices reached her very strangely, like voices at a service in a cathedral, since she was not following the words. The sudden gusts of laughter, and then one voice (Minta’s) speaking by itself, reminded her of men and boys calling out the Latin of a service in some Roman Catholic cathedral. She waited. Her husband was speaking. He was repeating something, and she could tell it was poetry from the rhythm and from the note of exaltation and sadness in his voice:
17.66:
Come out and climb the garden path,
Luriana Lurilee.
The China rose is all abloom and buzzing with the yellow bee.
17.67: The words (she was looking at the window) seemed to be floating out there like flowers on water, cut off from all of them, as though nobody had spoken them and they had simply come into being on their own.
17.68:
And all the lives we ever lived and all the lives to be
Are full of trees and changing leaves.
17.69: What they meant, she did not know; but the words, like music, seemed to be spoken in her own voice, somewhere outside her, saying quite easily and naturally what had been in her mind all evening while she was saying other things. Without looking around she knew that everyone at the table was listening to the voice as it said:
17.70:
I wonder if it seems to you
Luriana, Lurilee
17.71: and listening with the same relief and pleasure she felt, as if at last this were the natural thing to say, as if it were their own voice that was speaking.
17.72: Then the voice broke off. She looked around, and made herself stand up. Augustus Carmichael was on his feet, holding his napkin so that it hung like a long white robe, and he stood there chanting:
17.73:
To see the Kings go riding by
Over lawn and daisy lea
With their palm leaves and cedar sheaves,
Luriana, Lurilee,
17.74: and when she went past him he turned a little toward her and said the last words again:
17.76: and he bowed to her as though paying her homage. She did not know why, but she felt that he liked her better now than he ever had; and, relieved and grateful, she bowed back to him and went out through the door he was holding open for her.
17.77: Now everything had to be carried one step further. She stood with her foot on the threshold, lingering a moment more in a scene that was fading even as she watched it; then, as she moved and took Minta’s arm and left the room, it changed and took on a different shape. Glancing back at it one last time over her shoulder, she knew it had already become the past.
